SUMMER 1990

From An Owl
JVluch of this issue of the Diamond is devoted to the efforts
ofthe Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc., and the important role
that it plays in support of the Fraternity's educational efforts
for our undergraduates.
Many of you will, I am certain, have noted the series of
columns that Brother Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, current
Executive Director of the Foundation and former Executive
Vice President of the Fraternity, has written in the last few
issues of the Diamond concerning the history of the
Foundation's efforts. I do not intend to duplicate that informa
tion but do commend it to you if you have not previously had
a chance to read it. I do want to talk briefly, however, about
the cooperation that the Fraternity has received from the
Foundation over a long period of time, but particularly during
the period since July, 1987, when Brother Poor became the
first full-time Executive Director ofthe Foundation.
Although our Field Director program to provide direct
support to our chapters has been in existence since 1975, the
Foundation materially assisted our ability to add a second
full-time Field Director in 1983 through grants that it provided
for the educational aspects ofthat program. It has also provided
support for our administrative operations by sharing the costs
of duplication and telefax resources, computer facilities and
other joint operations so both organizations can reap some
economies of scale.
More recently, the leaders of the Fraternity and the Foun
dation met last fall to review the ongoing priorities of both
organizations in order to assure that our joint and separate
activities would allow the educational efforts of both organiza
tions to progress toward the same goals. That constructive
meeting resulted in agreement on six major joint goals:
(I) Leadership Conference �
initially for undergraduates
and ultimately to include alumni leaders as well, the Con
ference would provide training in the development of lead
ership skills and their application in a chapter setting;
(2) Values and Ethics Program �
focusing on the signifi
cant work done by the National Interfraternity Conference,
this program, as integrated into a variety of Fraternity activ
ities, would instill a strong sense of each individual chapter
member's responsibility to the Fratemity, the chapter, and
the educational institution (in Psi U's case, particularly to the
"highest social, intellectual, and moral excellence");
(3) Speakers Fund �
aimed at providing speakers for chap
ter and alumni events as well as our annual conventions and
leadership institutes;
(4) Chapter retreats �
providing an opportunity for each
of our chapters to have an annual weekend retreat to assess
where they are as a fraternity and where they should be going
during the next year;
(5) Headquarters building �
providing the funding for the
building or purchase of a headquarters building to house both
the Fraternity and the Foundation, thus allowing current
rental costs to be devoted to greater chapter and alumni
services;
(6) Alumni Services position �
similar to our current Di
rector of Chapter Services for undergraduates, this position
would focus on providing greater alumni services and support
for alumni activities.
The first of those priorities to be addressed by the Founda
tion and the Fraternity was the Leadership Institute (the
implementation title for "Leadership Conferences"), At the
December Executive Council meeting, the Fraternity ap
proved the submission of a
grant proposal to the Foundation
to conduct a Leadership Institute in conjunction with the
147th Convention in Atlanta in August, 1990, During early
1990, the Executive Directors ofthe Fratemity (including the
Field Directors) and the Foundation worked on the program
theme and topics for the proposed Leadership Institute and in
April, the Foundation's Board of Directors approved the con
cept, followed by specific authorization of the grant in June,
1990,
The first Leadership Institute had as its major theme
the nine principles that have evolved from the National Inter
fraternity Conference's Commission on Values and Ethics,
These nine principles apply to the day-to-day leadership chal
lenges facing our chapters (the second goal is thus also included
in the Leadership Institute concept at its inception). The
Foundation and Fraternity staffs found the finest speak
ers (where the third goal is also incorporated for the first time),
facilitators, and attendees possible to achieve the goals of this
program.
This effort, the first aimed at pursuing the joint goals agreed
upon last fall, demonstrates the close relationship that we are
fortunate to have in Psi Upsilon between the Fraternity and
the Foundation as we strive to improve our services to our
chapters and alumni alike. Great credit is due to Henry Poor,
Tom Phillips (our Acting Executive Director until Mark Wil
liams arrived in early June), and Mark Williams for their
extensive cooperative efforts in making the Institute a success!
Psi Upsilon is embarked upon a new and exciting path
toward providing to our members �
undergraduate and alumni
alike �
an even higher quality of experience as brothers than
was
previously possible. That path is open to us largely because
ofthe cooperative efforts that the Foundation and the Frater
nity have undertaken. On behalf of the Fraternity and the
Executive Council in particular, I want to thank the Founda
tion for its "spirit of brotherhood" that allows us to pass on to
those who are our undergraduate brothers and their future
generations of colleagues the same warm enthusiasm for the
special bonds of brotherhood we have in Psi Upsilon!
Yours in the bonds,
William R .
Robie,
Epsilon Omega '66 President

At the May 12, 1990 meeting of the
Executive Council, a
group of outstand
ing undergraduates at Miami University
in Oxford, Ohio was granted a Provisional
Chapter of Psi Upsilon. This group of 32
first contacted the intemational office in
the spring of 1989. After discussions with
the group over the past year, and numer
ous visits to Oxford, members ofthe Fra
temity staff and Executive Council were
more than confident that the group was
deserving of Provisional Chapter status.
Miami University is a
highly selective
state-supported institution of 12,000 un
dergraduates. Miami was established by
an act of the Ohio Ceneral Assembly in
1809 but did not officially open until 1824.
Named as one of the "Public Ivys" in a
recent book by Richard Moll, the school
boasts rigorous admissions standards, a
competitive academic atmosphere, and
one of the most scenic campuses in the
nation.
Several Fraternities were founded at
Miami including Sigma Chi, Phi Delta
Theta, Reta Theta Pi, Phi Kappa Tau, and
Delta Zeta Sorority. Fratemities are a
very strong tradition at this fine institu
tion, one in which Psi Upsilon should be
very proud to join.
Also May 12th the Executive Council
granted Provisional Chapter Status to a
group at the University ofTexas at Austin.
The group, formerly known as Chi Theta
Beta is composed of 26 undergraduates
formed in the fall of 1989. They were
seeking cultural diversity that could not
be found readily in other UT fraternities.
In the spring of 1990 they began looking
at international fratemities with which to
affiliate, and were drawn to Psi Upsilon.
The international office staff worked with
the group and quickly became very ex
cited about the outstanding caliber ofthe
members, especially their diversity of
membership.
This will be Psi Upsilon's first chapter
in the Southwest, and will be a catalyst for

future growth in that region. The school
is noted for its large endowment which
has an interesting story behind it: One
day in 1923 an oil well known as Santa Rita
One blew in the Premian Basin ofTexas �
the first to begin gushing on state-owned
land. The result was a flow of money into
a state education endowment that pro
pelled the University of Texas to a posi
tion second only to Harvard among the
nation's best-endowed universities.
With a total enrollment of over 47,000
students, this institution is also among the
largest single-campus institutions in the
country. The University ofTexas was also
named one ofthe "Public Ivys." Psi Up
silon is represented at five of the eight
schools identified as "Public Ivys." The
others are the University of California,
University of Michigan, Miami Univer
sity, and the College of William and

The academic strenghts of the Univer
sity of Texas include psychology, botany,
linguistics, Spanish, and accounting.
While engineering and computer science
are rated highly, as well.

At that the same historic meeting, a
group at Washington State University in
Pullman, Washington was granted Col
ony status. Colony status is one step to
achieving Provisional Chapter status. A
Provisional Chapter then petitions the
Fraternity as a whole to become an active
Chapter.
Contact with this group began in the
spring of 1990, when they contacted the
intemational office. The group of twenty
was founded to emphasize academics and
community service, something that they
were not finding in other WSU fraterni
ties. Once again the caliber of the mem
bers is outstanding. They contacted a
number of fratemities before deciding
that it was Psi Upsilon with which they
were most interested in affiliating.
The competitive, public supported,
school of 16,000 students was founded in
1890. From its founding, liberal arts and
sciences have occupied an important
place in the curriculum, along with busi
ness, education, nursing, pharmacy; and,
as the State's land grant institution, agri
culture, home economics, veterinary
medicine and engineering.
1990 will go down in the Annals of Psi
Upsilon as a banner year for not since
1843 has Psi Upsilon attempted to found
three new chapters in the same year.
These three groups were attracted by
Psi Upsilon's tradition, its impressive his
tory, and its diversity. These same values
are cherished by every generation of Psi
U's.
SPEAKING OF
THE FOUNDATION
The First Thirty Years (continued)
Faithful readers will recall previous editions of this column,
chronicling the birth of The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. three
decades ago, its gradual development during the first twenty-odd
years, and, its "taking off" when the Sesquicentennial Fund was
launched in 1982.
It wasn't very long after the start of this ambitious fund-raising
effort when talks with major alumni prospects revealed a critical
need by several Chapters to finance repairs and renovations to their
aging physical structures. All agree that this must be a top priority.
The Foundation directors recognize that the primary Psi U
interest of every alumnus (without exception in my experience)
quite properly focuses on his own Chapter. Their challenge, then,
was how to off'er assistance to these needy Chapters and at the same
time to advance the cause of the Sesquicentennial Fund. Clearly
the Chapters' plight must be addressed first. And in a broad sense
our objectives are the same. For what benefits an individual Chapter
likewise benefits the Fraternity as a whole.
Out of the Board deliberations, and from discussions with attor
neys and tax consultants, there emerged a creative plan for cooper
ative fund-raising by the Foundation and Chapter alumni
organizations. The program was not to be "pushed" but simply to
be made available to any Chapters which felt this to be their most
desirable alternative and in their best interests.
Paramount among its advantages is the feature of gifts to the
Foundation being tax deductible, not generally possible for gifts
directly to the Chapter. A second benefit is the active participation
of the Foundation's executive director in solicitation visits as he
travels around the country. Still another in this program is the
involvement without cost ofthe Foundation's professional fund-rais
ing consultant. Finally, in a coordinated undertaking the Chapter's
alumni need be solicited only once, rather than separately, for both
Psi U organizations.
Balanced against these advantages, the Chapter must weigh
whether its total contributions may be greater by conducting its own
campaign with volunteer effort, or whether the results will be
increased by the setting of higher sights in a joint program.
With a cooperative fund-raising plan the proceeds are divided
between the Chapter and the Foundation. A forty per cent fundraising fee is paid to the Chapter as funds are received by the
Foundation. An additional amount of up to ten per cent can be
obtained by the Chapter petitioning the Foundation for a grant
meeting educational standards. If a Chapter's need is more imme
diate, payments of pledges can be weighted in that direction.
Our next column will discuss the Chapters which have opted for
this cooperative program to date, as well as variations to this formula
developed to meet special Chapter situations.
Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39
Foundation Executive Director

Wall dismantled, the borders ofEastern Europe
opened, and realized the probability ofa unified
Germany. Six years before the Iron Curtain fell,
Robert Noworyta, Zeta '92, undertook a two
year run to freedom. At the age of 15, Brother
Noworyta (pronounced no-WAR-ta) defected
from his native Poland, surviving essentially on
his own wit and guile. Rob's flight to the West
and to freedom began after he was twice ar
rested in Gdansk, Poland for marching in sup
port of Solidarity causes.
"In most cases when parents know there's
going to be a march, they keep their kids in
side,
"
Brother Noworyta explained. "There's a
lot of kids missing. But my mother didn't stop

Brother Noworyta, now a tennis player at
Dartmouth, was then ranked 13th in Poland's
16-and-under age group. It was during a visit
by an Austrian tennis coach that Rob first
thought about defecting to the West. The coach
wanted Rob to train in Austria but he was de
nied an exit visa. "That planted the idea to
defect. There's no future for young people in
Poland. I was
looking for something better."
Wikoria Noworyta, Rob's mother, helped
him obtain an illegal passport through a friend
in the government. An aunt who worked for
Solidarity told him how to contact the under
ground in Czechoslovakia once there.
It was mid-winter when the 15-year-old Rob
ert Noworyta began his odyssey. With a back
pack, 2 tennis racquets, and $500, Rob left his
native Poland. "My mom was very nervous
when I left, but she was happy for me.
"
Brother Noworyta and a friend hid behind
boxes stacked in the back of an 18-wheeI tractor
trailer. The ride ended in Czechoslovakia where
the underground was to take the pair over the
mountains and across the Yugoslavian border.
In the mountains Rob and his companion
were joined by four others. Like a scene from a
John LeCarre novel, the group was spotted by
Czech border guards. There followed a footrace
to the border. Fortunately the border guards
"couldn't do anything because we were too far
away. We

Rob then encountered Robbie Suydam, man

Suydam took him in and gave Rob a place to

Brother Robert L. Kaiser, Zeta '39, observed

of all the fine Zeta undergraduate brothers I

"
This is considerable praise indeed coming from
an Executive Council member, a past Psi Upsi
lon Foundation President, and an Honorary

Brother Kaiser and his wife, Evelyn, met with
Rob before writing in support of Rob's scholar
ship application. Brother Kaiser noted: "When
we asked why Robert joined Psi Upsilon, he
explained that when he came to Dartmouth he
had no friends whatsoever at the College and
felt very much alone. As a consequence, he felt
that by joining a fraternity, he could acquire a
group ofclose friends and find a home. (Remem
ber that he has no home other than Dartmouth. )
During informal rush among the various frater
nities, Robert was impressed with the type of
brotherhood he saw at Psi U, and was very
pleased to accept a bid.
"
Brother Noworyta's concern for Psi Upsilon
led to his election as Assistant House Manager,
one of the few elected positions available to
members of his class. Darren Keefe, Zeta '91,
chapter president commented that "Robert was
always doing things around the house even if no
one asked. As an officer whose responsibilities
are often both herculean and, sadly, unappreci
ated, Rob has taken great satisfaction in ensur
ing that the Zeta Chapter's physical plant is in
the best shape it can be."
Brother Kai
ser noted: "De
spite the heavy
demand on his
time for studies,
his mandatory
em pi oy m en t

nity, Robert

Dartmouth var

In view of his

I suspect that he
will be playing near the top of the ladder this

"
The most insightful comment came from
Darren Keefe: "If Psi Upsilon's Zeta Chapter is
to continue to be a leader on the Dartmouth
campus it needs men like Robert Noworyta. In
the world of Ivy League academia (where ac
tions are often prompted solely by materialistic
concerns) it is refreshing, and, I think, neces
sary to encounter someone whose entire life has
been guided by the pursuit of a higher goal.
Unarguably, Rob is such a person."
While the world rejoices in the recent devel
opments in Eastern Europe, we must not forget
the stories of individual bravery, heroism, and
sacrifice in the name of freedom. Brother
Noworyta's run to freedom is one such story.

FOUNDATION AWARDS 42
SCHOLARSHIPS FOR 1990-91
The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. ,
at its April
17, 1990 meeting unanimously voted to award
scholarship grants to 42 deserving undergradiiates. Recipients from twenty-six chapters (plus
four special recipients) received grants totalling
$42,150.
Beginning with a modest grant of $30 in 1959,
the Scholarship Program has given over 500
grants in the past 30 years totalling over
$350,000.
A scholarship committee composed of Henry
B. Poor, Gamma '39, Chairman; David A.B.
Brov\^n, Epsilon Phi '66; Travis B. Jacobs,
Lambda '62; R. Timothy Leedy, Phi '57; and
George T. Sewall, Kappa '32, works diligently
each year insuring the overwhelming success of
this program. Each applicant submits materials
including references and a college transcript.
The members of the Scholarship Committee
review the extensive amount of materials to
determine not only who should receive an
award, but the amount of the grant.
Congratulations to the recipients ofthe 199091 scholarship grants.
